narrative: The first delta in the series sets the baseline: the active count rose from 823,658 to 837,789, a net of +14,131. That modest number hides a lot of churn — 26,768 codes added against 12,637 removed, the highest removal count of any release as Statistics Canada pruned a backlog of retired codes.

Growth was led by Alberta, which added 9,048 codes — more than Ontario's 6,364 despite a third of the population, the fingerprint of the province's post-2021 population and construction boom. Removals, by contrast, were an Ontario/Quebec story (4,838 and 3,984).

The real place-name changes are few (1,313) but include the dataset's most famous rename: Asbestos, Quebec → Val-des-Sources (502 codes, plus 75 to neighbouring Danville) — the town's 2020 vote to shed the mineral's name finally reaching the address file. In Ontario, 570 codes shifted from Windsor to Tecumseh as the suburb's boundary was recognised.

Encoding noise is essentially absent this cycle (359) — the great mojibake wave doesn't arrive until mid-2024. What is already stirring is municipality recoding: 9,197 CSD reassignments, concentrated in Ontario (4,503) and New Brunswick (2,175).

added: Alberta out-adding Ontario in absolute terms is the standout. It matches the province's 2022–23 in-migration and housing surge — new subdivisions in the Calgary–Edmonton corridor generating fresh delivery codes faster than anywhere else.
removed: The highest removals in the series. This early release looks like a clean-up pass — Statistics Canada retiring codes that had lingered in the file, concentrated in the two largest, longest-established provinces.
substantive: Asbestos → Val-des-Sources is a genuine civic renaming (a 2020 referendum), not a boundary or encoding artefact — the clearest case in the whole dataset of a real place deliberately changing its name.
